Regarding the twelve *dhūta* practices: the first is not to accept invitations from others, but to go on almsround daily, nor to accept even a single portion of food or any money from the community of monks.
Second, one should lodge on mountains and not stay in human dwellings, such as districts, counties, or villages.

Third, one must not beg for clothing from others; even if people offer clothing, one shall not accept it, but instead take only the discarded clothes left by the dead in burial mounds to mend and wear.
Fourth, dwelling in wild fields or beneath trees.
Fifth, eating only one meal per day, also known as *saṃghāṇi*.
Sixth, remaining seated throughout the day and night without lying down; when sleepiness comes, one rises and practices walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), also known as *naiṣadyika*.
Seventh, he possesses three robes and no others, nor does he lie within a bedding.
Eighth, he dwells among burial mounds, neither in a Buddhist temple nor among the populace; gazing upon the skeletal remains of the dead, he sits in meditation to seek the Way.
Ninth, they desire only to dwell alone and do not wish to see others, nor do they wish to lie down with others.
Tenth, they first eat fruits and melons and only afterwards eat rice; once they have finished eating, they must not eat fruit again.
Eleventh, he desires only to sleep in the open air, not dwelling under trees or in houses.
Twelfth, he does not eat meat nor does he consume clarified butter (ghṛta), and he does not apply sesame oil to his body.
There are twenty-five reasons for carrying the *khakkhara* staff:
first, for the sake of insects on the ground;
second, for the sake of old age.
Third, for the sake of begging for alms;
fourth, when entering or exiting and seeing a Buddha image, one must not allow the head to make a sound;
fifth, one must not enter the assembly carrying a staff.
Sixth, after midday, one must not go out again carrying a staff.
Seventh, one must not carry it on the shoulder.
Eighth, one must not place it horizontally across the shoulder with the hands hanging from both ends.
Ninth, one must not swing the staff back and forth with the hands.
Tenth, one must not carry the staff to the rear of the dwelling.
Eleventh, once the three teachers have exited carrying their staffs, one must not follow them out while also carrying a staff.
Twelfth: If four people travel together and one person goes out carrying a staff, the others may not follow behind carrying staffs as well.
Thirteenth: Upon arriving at the house of a donor, one must not be separated from the staff.
Fourteenth: When arriving at a person's door, one should cough three times; if they do not come out, one should simply depart and go elsewhere.
Fifteenth: Should the person come out, one should place the staff upon the left elbow and hold it there.
Sixteenth: When the staff is inside the room, one must not allow it to touch the ground.
Seventeenth: One should keep it close to one's own bed.
Eighteenth: One should take it up and wipe it clean.
Nineteenth: One must not allow hair to grow on the head.
Twentieth: When wishing to go out carrying a staff, one should receive it from a śrāmaṇera or from a layperson (avadātavasana).
Twenty-first: When arriving at the home of one who is ill or emaciated for lodging, one should obtain a staff in the evening.
Twenty-second: when escorting someone a long distance, one should receive an evening staff.
Twenty-third: when inviting someone to stay overnight at a distant location, one should receive an evening staff.
Twenty-fourth: when traveling on the *ākiyūn* (a long journey), one should receive an evening staff.
Twenty-fifth: One should always keep [this precept] close to oneself; one must not point at people or draw figures or write characters on the ground.
There are five occasions when one should go to the house of an upāsaka:
first, on a mission for the Saṃgha; second, for alms-round (piṇḍapāta); third, for *ācārya*; fourth, for an invitation to a meal; and fifth, in cases of illness or death.
In all other cases, one should not go.
There are five matters regarding a bhikṣu preaching the sūtras to an upāsikā:
first, if an upāsikā comes with a small child in her arms to ask about the sūtras, he should not preach with lustful intentions.
Second, if a lustful intention arises, one must not go forward to take hold of a small child and fondle them.
Third, one must not pull [the child] to sit beside oneself.

Fourth, if an upāsikā requests that a bhikṣu recite the *Tailadhārā-sūtra*, she should have a man hold a *yācī* (tooth-stick) for the bhikṣu; it is proper to hold the *yācī* from the man's hand, and one should not speak [of such matters].
Fifth, if an upāsaka and an upāsikā come together to inquire about the sūtras, the bhikṣu should also go out if the upāsaka departs first; otherwise, it is contrary to the Dharma.
A newly arrived bhikṣu has ten duties:
first, having paid homage to the Buddha, he should stand back and inquire after the name of the *karmadāna*, the number of bhikṣus in the saṃgha, and his own name for the day’s observance.
Second, those of higher rank should pay homage, while those of lower rank should inquire after their well-being.
Third, one must not ask where they reside.
Fourth, when others provide a bhikṣu with bedding, mats, or sleeping requisites, one must not criticize them as being good or poor.
Fifth, one should seek to rely upon an ācārya.
Sixth, one should likewise make offerings to him.
Seventh, one must not revile the sūtras.
Eighth, one must not enter or exit at will.
Ninth, if one wishes to sweep the stūpa, one should inform Māpali.
Tenth, when about to depart, if there are bedding and seating materials, one should entrust them to the host.

Furthermore, there are five matters: first, one should concern oneself with communal affairs; second, one must not recklessly use the pure water within the monastery; third, one must not recklessly enter the private chambers of others; fourth, one must not walk against the flow of the path; and fifth, one must not step over the staffs or wooden railings within the monastery.
One should attend to newly arrived bhikṣus with ten matters:
first, one should avoid giving them a room;
second, one should provide what they require.
Third, one should go to visit and inquire after them morning and evening.
Fourth, one should speak of the customs and practices of their native land.
Fifth, one should instruct them on matters of taboo and avoidance.
Sixth, one should inform him of the place where alms are sought.
Seventh, one should inform him of the instructions given by the Sangha.
Eighth, one should inform him of what may be eaten.
Ninth, one should inform the local authorities of prohibitions.
Tenth, one should inform them of bandits and thieves, specifying which are permitted for escape and which are not.
When a newly arrived bhikṣu wishes to go to a worthy person to take refuge and accept them as his *upādhyāya* (preceptor), he should first speak thus:
“I am now [named so-and-so], who has distanced myself from my three teachers, each of whom resides several *li* away.
I have come here alone; my original intention was to study, but as successive rulers were unsettled, I have come to this place.”
I now take refuge in the Venerable One; may you act as my preceptor for dependence (*niśrayācārya*).

Because of my taking refuge in you, O Venerable One, please accept me, [Name], as your disciple. I shall dwell together with [Name] as your disciple, rely upon [Name] in our shared residence, and serve as [Name]'s disciple.
"Venerable one, for the sake of the Dharma, you should act as the preceptor (ācārya) for [Name].
Having prostrated with his head at [the other's] feet, he then said: "Preceptor!"
For the sake of the Triple Gem, you have already accepted so-and-so as your teacher; you shall now instruct so-and-so in the methods of conduct for entering and leaving.
If there should be anyone who forcibly disputes with so-and-so, the Acharya must ensure that so-and-so acts as his disciple.
Whether the ācārya or the candidate wishes to depart or remain, both shall have full autonomy.
Even if the candidate departs and subsequently returns from that person's presence, the ācārya must still accept the candidate as his disciple.
When he has spoken thus up to three times, the teacher shall reply:

"Venerable [Name], listen now to what I say, so that you may attain the Way. You must always act according to the Buddha’s words: you must guard the precepts; you must practice patience; you must exert diligence; you must single-mindedly contemplate the Way; you must contemplate wisdom; you must restrain body, speech, and mind to extinguish the poisons; and you must perform the three dharmic duties."
"Having already become disciples of the Buddha, you must not think of or engage in worldly affairs.
Those who are able to practice according to the Dharma will surely attain the Way and transcend the world.
Having finished speaking, he ceased.
Having arisen and paid homage, he should place his head at the feet of the teacher and depart; then, taking up his robes and bowl, he goes to the preceptor from whom he received the robes.
If a bhikṣu receives robes and bowls—the three sets of robes—the ācārya bhikṣu must personally declare their loss or destruction due to causes such as water, fire, or thieves.
The bhikṣu first makes his own declaration, saying:
"Venerable sir! The wise one whose conduct is pure and whose precepts are purified is my third teacher."

Having thus stated the original cause three times for such-and-such a person, and having further stated it three times, he ascends to receive the bowl or the robe from the ācārya, and then delivers the instruction:
"Listen, worthy one!
Human beings possess the six sense-faculties; they should be guarded and kept pure through mindfulness.

Although worldly cleanliness cannot lead to true purity, the practitioner of wisdom must guard both internal and external purity on the Path. When one is free from defilement and leakage, with the internal and external in harmony, this is what enables one to reach the Path of Purity. Therefore, one should rely upon, collect oneself within, and guard these faculties.
Regarding this matter of the alms-bowl, one should say: "It should be held and inspected frequently, worn at the proper times, and washed at the proper times.
A bhikṣu, like a noble person dwelling in the world, delights in bathing, incense, clothing, and bedding; how could he wish for his body to be ill at ease or his mind to be ill at ease?
All those things that are pleasing, even if they consist of tattered robes, do not provide firm security;
nor can they lead one upon the path to pure wisdom.

If it becomes moist with secretions and is eaten by worms until it rots—just as if one part of the body were to rot and decay—from that point on there is no peace, and one does not reach the path of the wise.
If one part of the body is eaten by worms, becoming a sore, or painful, or itchy—just as such a case—therefrom there is no peace, and one does not reach the path of the wise.

From beginning to end, relying upon and guarding the internal and external cleansing is the means to eliminate greed and practice fewness of desires, thereby bringing about the purity of the noble ones.
This is the matter of reliance.
There are fifteen matters by which an ācārya instructs his disciple:
first, when the community of bhikṣus assembles, he should instruct him to observe the order of seniority according to the Dharma.
Second, there are the instructions issued by the community of bhikṣus which one must not transgress.
Third, one should be taught to follow the seniority within the community.
Fourth, one should be taught to practice reverence.
Fifth, one should inform them of the local customs and taboos of the country, as well as what foods may be eaten and what should not be eaten.
Sixth, one should inform them of the regions, specifying which places may be visited and which places must not be visited.
Seventh, if there are thieves or robbers, [he shall indicate] which places are safe to flee to and which are not.
Eighth, if one is sick or emaciated, he shall examine and attend to them.
Ninth, if clothing or bedding is ruined, he shall provide replacements.
Tenth, if there are those who come or go, one must not obstruct or hinder them.
Eleventh, one should observe the intentions of others.
Twelfth, one should dwell according to skillful means.
Thirteenth, when someone comes to question you, you should respond with deference.
Fourteenth, when wishing to sprinkle water upon the ground, one should always act with humility and yield.
Fifteenth, even if you have committed a fault, you must not say, "I will no longer speak with you."
This is the method for relying upon an ācārya.
There are five matters regarding a disciple’s reliance upon an ācārya: first, one should go to him frequently;

second, upon reaching his door, one should snap the fingers three times; third, having entered, one should prostrate with the head to the ground; fourth, kneeling for a long time, one should inquire after his well-being; fifth, when departing, one should turn back toward the door before leaving.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, one should go morning and evening to inquire after [the teacher's] well-being;
second, when the teacher calls, one must immediately don the *kāṣāya* and go to respond, and must not enter alone wearing sandals.
Third, one should sweep the floor, prepare water for washing, and wipe down the bedding and mats;
fourth, whether one has tasks of one's own to perform or when entering, leaving, walking, or staying, one should inform [the teacher];
fifth, when going to receive the scriptures or inquire about their meaning, whether one succeeds or fails, one should not harbor feelings of fear.
These are the five matters concerning the method of relying upon one's own preceptor.
A wise bhikṣu should not keep seven kinds of medicines:

first, medicines for avoiding grain; second, medicines for digesting grain; third, medicines for inducing vomiting or purging; fourth, medicines for strengthening virility; fifth, elixirs for nourishing the body; sixth, poisons; and seventh, medicines for treating wounds from weapons.
When there is no illness, one should not take medicine at all, nor should one give it to others to take; to do so constitutes an offense.
There are five matters by which a bhikṣu may raise the status of a śrāmaṇera:
first, he should know the four Āgamas; second, he should know the precepts; third, he should know the sūtras; fourth, he should possess wisdom; and fifth, he should possess virtue.

Furthermore, there are five matters: first, one should uphold the precepts; second, one should not violate the precepts; third, one should be able to understand the sutras; fourth, one should practice patience; and fifth, one should maintain self-restraint in all things.
Only one who possesses these qualities may ordain a śrāmaṇera;
if one does not fully know them, one should not raise a śrāmaṇera.
A bhikṣu who has a śrāmaṇera should instruct him in five matters:
First, while a śrāmaṇera is engaged in communal tasks and has not yet finished them, one must not summon him;
second, one must not cause a śrāmaṇera to seek out the faults of virtuous persons;
third, one must not place trust in the words of a śrāmaṇera.
Fourth, one must not shout at a śrāmaṇera in the midst of the assembly;
fifth, one must not assign him tasks alone, but should instead have him provide for the affairs of the community.
There are three matters for which one should not dwell together with a śrāmaṇera:

First, those who are fond of physical beauty; second, those who become angry upon seeing [the practitioner]; third, those who are afflicted by illness. There are three matters for which one should be expelled:

first, those who claim that violating the precepts incurs no fault; second, those who claim that the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha do not exist; third, those who go about telling others the good or bad qualities of their own preceptors (upādhyāya) and instructors (ācārya).
If one wishes to travel far and entrusts a *śrāmaṇera* to another person, there are five matters to be observed:
first, one must first ask whether the *śrāmaṇera* is to your liking;
second, one must ask whether you can serve your host in a manner that is pleasing to them.
Third, even if they should scold or revile you, you must not say, "This is not my ācārya; he reviles me unjustly.
Fourth, serve your master as if you were serving me.
Fifth, when they instruct you according to the Dharma, you must not abandon them and depart.
When a novice is brought before the host and permission is granted for him to stay as a dependent, there are five matters:
first, one should teach him to perform prostrations with his head to the ground.
Second, instructing them to take refuge;
third, saying, "You shall regard me, a śrāmaṇera, as you would your own śrāmaṇera";
fourth, that when I return from my journey, they shall naturally return to me.
Fifth, if I am no longer present, you shall have long-term charge of him.
There are five matters regarding the reception of a novice (śrāmaṇera) as a dependent:

first, one must teach him to recite the scriptures; second, one must teach him not to violate the precepts; third, one must teach him how to follow the assembly in ascending and descending; fourth, one must teach him the rules for walking; fifth, one must teach him to show respect to all people.
When the community of bhikṣus takes their meal, there are five matters to observe:

first, one must not sit before the elder (sthavira) has sat; second, one must not receive food from the tray before the elder has received his; third, one must not begin eating before the elder has begun eating; fourth, one must not stop eating before the elder has finished eating; fifth, one must not rise before the elder has risen.
There are five matters regarding the receiving of a table:

first, one should receive it while holding a hand-towel; second, one should set its width at one chi and six cun; third, one should hold the hand-towel connected to the legs of the table or desk; fourth, one should draw back the knees; fifth, both elbows must not leave the knees.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, once you have received [the precepts], do not abandon them;
second, you must not look around frantically to the left or right.
Third, having already departed, one should receive [the meal] from the elder;
fourth, even if there are people who are unsuitable, one must not fail to eat;
fifth, if someone with whom one has long been incompatible should be present, one may employ skillful means or summon others oneself.

Furthermore, there are five matters: first, one must not carry anything in either the left or right hand; second, one must not shout loudly when seeking something; third, when giving a bowl to another, one should look up and down and face the person before handing it over; fourth, when giving a bowl, one should support the top with the right hand; fifth, one should protect that which has been received.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, when someone comes to give you an object, you should wash your hands again once their hand is near;
second, you must not hold it directly over the bowl and place it inside.
Third, if one sees food that is disagreeable, one should not eat it, nor should one allow those around one to know of it;
fourth, one must not spit upon the elder (upādhyāya) while eating;
fifth, one commits an offense if one eats when one should not eat.

Furthermore, there are five matters: first, one must not rub or wipe the face or eyes with the hands; second, once the left hand is soiled, it must not be brought near the right hand; third, if the hands are already soiled, one must not take up water from the alms bowl; fourth, one must not use soiled hands to straighten the *kāṣāya*; fifth, one must not use a hand-towel to wipe greasy hands.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, if the cup placed before one is tilted, it should be straightened; if it is not straight, one must not eat.
Second, once eating utensils have fallen, one should not eat further.
Third, if someone comes to provide benefit, one should always support them with one's finger;
fourth, one should not eat if the person who brought the food is not seen;
fifth, when food is placed before one, one must not taste it beforehand.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, one must not pass wind while seated during a meal;
second, one must not spit upon the ground before oneself while the meal is not yet finished.
Third, if one urgently wishes to spit, one should spit beneath the sandals;
fourth, once the hands have been washed, one must not again take up the sandals;
fifth, once the sandals have been taken up and one knows the hands are soiled, if they are not wiped clean, one must not use them to hold the *kāṣāya*.
The above are the forty matters concerning eating.
Regarding the five matters for washing and rinsing after a meal: first, one must not rub one's hands on the bowl;

second, one must not use the fingers to pick at or stir within the mouth; third, one must not blow the nose or spit excessively into the bowl; fourth, when rinsing the mouth, one must not allow rice grains to remain and spit them back into the bowl; fifth, one must not shake the hands violently, splashing water upon those nearby.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, when holding a hand-towel, one must not teach it to be soft; rather, one should first practice handling it until it is well-versed in the motions.
Second, one must not shake out a wet towel to take up a dry one.
Third, one must not wipe the face, eyes, nose, or mouth with the hands;
fourth, one must not say "this is mine" and fail to take it away;
fifth, one should use it in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, once the hands have been dried by wiping, one should immediately store the hand-towel upon one's knees;
second, having done so, one should straighten the *kāṣāya*, and must not drape it over those standing to the left or right.
Third, while the junior monks have not yet finished washing their feet, one must not scold them to make them come forward;
fourth, during the daily *dakṣiṇā*, one must not engage in idle chatter;
fifth, until the *dakṣiṇā* has concluded, one must not rise from one's seat abruptly.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, if the *upādhyāya* (elder) is preaching the sūtras for a donor (*dānapati*), one should listen while sitting upright;
second, if one wishes to leave urgently to attend to communal affairs, one must pass by and inform the *mopoli* (karmadāna).
Third, if one urgently wishes to send a messenger to the east or west, one should inform those seated below;
fourth, if one receives a share of money, one should immediately inspect and store it away;
fifth, if there is something to be returned or entrusted to another, one must not push it with one’s feet nor throw it from a distance.
Regarding the ten matters concerning the rice: when looking left and right, there is no [action] that does not involve fault.
First, one should observe whether the elder (upādhyāya) has received his tray;
second, one should observe whether the offerings have been fully prepared before the elder.
Third, one should likewise observe the junior monks;
fourth, while everyone is eating, one should repeatedly observe them to see if the senior monk has received less than others, and if there are any who have finished, call for more to be served;
fifth, one should likewise observe the junior monks.
Sixth, while the meal has not yet concluded, one should pause to look and ask the senior monk what he desires;
seventh, one should do the same when looking at the junior monks;
eighth, one should observe whether the senior monks have finished eating; even if one has finished first, one must hold the food remaining before oneself and must not sit down to watch others.
Ninth, one should look down at those seated below in the same manner;
tenth, one must not take up the table first, but should push it aside and hold it while waiting for others.
There are twenty-five matters regarding a bhikṣu holding the *piṇḍapātra* bowl:
First, if the hands are not clean, one must not grasp the upper ornament;
second, if the hands are not clean, one must not grasp the upper lid;
third, if the hands are not clean, one must not grasp the front opening.
Fourth, if the hands are not clean, one must not be made to add water;
fifth, if the hands are not clean, one must not grasp the front of the neck;
sixth, one should support the abdomen from below.
Seventh, if the water is scarce, one should merely wash the hands slightly to make them clean;
eighth, one should go out to add more water and return to pour it on well;
ninth, when wishing to add water for washing, one should first pour water over it three times to cleanse it thoroughly.
Tenth, when wishing to pour water, one should empty the vessel three times, refill it, and carry it inside;
eleventh, when carrying it inside, one must not stand in the middle of the path;
twelfth, one should place it in a secluded spot.
Thirteenth, one should always ensure that the lower part has branches;
fourteenth, one should install the upper cover straight and level;
fifteenth, one should leave it overnight filled with water.
Sixteenth, when holding the basin for washing, one must not drag it so that it makes a sound;
seventeenth, one must not allow the upper edge to become soiled;
eighteenth, one must not allow rice to remain inside.
Nineteenth, one should discard impure water;
twentieth, when discarding water, one should not go too far and should pour it out slowly with the hand;
twenty-first, when washing a basin, one should first wash both the inside and outside until it is thoroughly clean.
Twenty-second: When holding the washing basin with unwashed hands, one must not stop midway to hold it while rinsing the mouth;
twenty-third: when holding the washing basin with soiled hands, one must not grasp the *bimban* (face-washing stand) to wipe the mouth;
twenty-fourth: one must not take water from beneath the hearth to wash the *bimban*.
Twenty-fifth: both inside and outside, one must wash three times with water before being permitted to enter.
If one wishes to place a *piṇḍapātra* (alms bowl) upon a stand, one must not drop it down forcefully so that it makes a sound.
When using a hand-towel, there are five matters to attend to:
first, one should wipe both the upper and lower parts of the head;
second, one should use one end to wipe the hands and the other end to wipe the face and eyes.
Third, one must not use it to wipe the nose;
fourth, if it becomes stained with grease or filth from its use, it should be washed immediately;
fifth, one must not use it to wipe the body; for bathing, one should each have their own towel.
When putting on the saṃghāṭī, there are five matters regarding the holding of the hand-towel:
first, one must not allow the ends of the towel to hang down and become visible;
second, one must not hold a white towel.
Third, one should cause discolored food to turn black;
fourth, one must not wipe the face;
fifth, when eating, one should cover the knees with the robe, and once the meal is finished, one should remove it.
If he does not leave, when someone comes to pay respects or rises to depart, he should first take the bedding and fold it away.
There are seven types of monks in the *bhikṣu-saṃgha* who should not serve as *mopali* (steward) or on duty:

first, those too old to perform tasks; second, those suffering from illness, rashes, or sores and thus lacking cleanliness; third, those long ill and extremely emaciated; fourth, those whom the community collectively employs to nurse the sick; fifth, the day of the *upādhyāya* (preceptor); sixth, the *karmadāna* (work-manager); and seventh, the *varṣika* (one responsible for the year’s duties).
These seven persons should not be treated as such; if they are stubborn or, like those who turn away and do not wish to act, they should not be rebuked or questioned.
They are, in fact, the treasures and hidden gems of future generations.
One who serves as the *pāṭimokkha-uposatha* officer should practice one hundred and sixty virtues;
one who serves as the monthly director (*māsa-vārika*) should practice sixty virtues;
and one who serves as the daily director (*divasa-vārika*) should practice ten virtues.
One who acts as a *māmaka* (steward) should practice thirty virtues;
one who acts as the *vaihāyasa* (yearly overseer) should practice ten virtues.
If these five types of persons act according to the above [teachings], they will before long attain the path of the unconditioned that transcends the world.
The *pāṇisamapāli* has fifteen virtues: first, because it is for the sake of the Buddha;
second, because it is for the sake of the Dharma.
Third, for the sake of the community of bhikṣus;
fourth, one should cherish the property of the assembly;
fifth, one should cherish the property of the saṃgha of the four quarters.
Sixth, one should cherish the property of the bhikṣu-saṃgha;
seventh, one should understand matters pertaining to the Buddha;
eighth, one should understand matters pertaining to the saṃgha of the four quarters.
Ninth, one should know the affairs of the community of bhikṣus;
tenth, one must not take property belonging to a stūpa and place it among the property of the *caitya* (Skt. *cāturdiśa*) saṃgha;
eleventh, one must not take property belonging to a stūpa and place it among the property of the community of bhikṣus.
Twelfth, one must not take the property of the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* and place it among the property of the stūpa;
thirteenth, one must not take the property of the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* and place it among the property of the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*;
fourteenth, one must not take the property of the *bhikṣu-saṃgha* and place it among the property of the stūpa.
Fifteenth: One must not take the property of the Bhikṣu Saṃgha and place it within the *cāturmāsika* (the property of the four-month retreat).
Furthermore, there are fifteen virtues regarding the property of the Saṃgha:
First, when one wishes to undertake any action, one should inform and report it to the assembly.
Second, one must not seize communal property and conceal it for private use.
Third, one must not use the property of the community to privately benefit those who are close or dear to oneself.
Fourth, one must not take property from the community and secretly bestow it upon others under a false name.
Fifth, one should regularly inspect and maintain the bedding and utensils of the various households.
Sixth, if anyone is ill, one should attend to them, providing whatever they require according to their needs.
Seventh, one should respectfully look after and serve the community of bhikṣus.
Eighth, when preparing food for the community of bhikṣus, one should ensure it is pure and clean.
Ninth, one should act in accordance with the wishes of the brāhmaṇas.
Tenth, it is just like serving spirits; there is no difference.
Eleventh, one must not give way to anger or joy.
Twelfth, desiring to practice purity, one must not work in the kitchen with the body exposed.
Thirteenth, at sunset, one should always rise and personally inspect the doors and gates, checking whether the doors of all the bhikṣus are closed.
If you encounter someone who appears unusual, do not immediately rebuke them;
instead, ask, "Are you a śramaṇa?
Once they have confirmed it, you should wait until the following day.
Fourteenth, one must not sweep from a cold place onto a hot place.
Fifteenth, one must not sweep from a hot place onto a cold place.
These constitute the fifteen matters.
The *karmadāna* in charge of monastic affairs should observe twenty-five virtues within the hall at the time of the meal:
first, once the empty seats have been arranged, he must personally go around and inspect them all to ensure they are entirely clean.
Second, one must not set out empty trays beforehand.
Third, when the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) has already received his portion of rice, [the distribution may proceed].
Fourth, in all distributions of items, they must reach as far as the *śrāmaṇeras* (novices), or be accepted by lay followers (*avadātavasana*).
Fifth, while the three masters are present, one must not perform rites for increase (*puṣṭi*).
Sixth, when dividing the portions into upper and lower sections, they must be made equal.
Seventh, when dividing the rice, one should personally use one’s hands to ensure it is level.
Eighth, when wishing to divide the soup, one should stir the ladle three times before pouring it out.
Ninth, one must ensure that the broth and the dregs are well-mixed.
Tenth, one must not place the soup directly from the cauldron into another's bowl; in all cases, one should first transfer it into a separate vessel.
Eleventh, one must not speak or laugh while holding a portion of food.
Twelfth, one must not call out from afar, saying, "Bring such-and-such here.
Thirteenth, if there is someone in the assembly who does not eat soup, one should provide them with what is suitable for them.
Fourteenth: If there is anyone in the assembly with whom one does not get along, one must not immediately revile or scold them while still seated.
Fifteenth: One must urgently keep in mind the care of the sick.
Sixteenth: When people bring food during the mealtime, one should distribute it immediately until it is exhausted; one must not say, "This should be reserved for a later day.
Seventeenth: One should serve the soup first when it is urgent.
Eighteenth: One must quickly increase the midday meal until it is exhausted.
Nineteenth: One must not stop midway to sit and watch the Sangha.
Twentieth: One must not distance oneself from the Sangha by stepping out in front of them.
Twenty-first: When everyone has finished eating, one should personally inspect what is lacking and look to see how much more should be added.
Twenty-second: One must not remain standing and call out loudly for attendants to check on the food and utensils before departing.
Twenty-third: When closing the storehouse, do not allow it to make a sound, nor should one discard anything on the ground.
Twenty-fourth: One should instruct people to prepare brooms, water for washing, and hand-towels in advance.
Twenty-fifth: One should remain and wait until the monks have finished receiving their offerings; only after personally announcing that it is concluded should one depart.
There are twenty-five virtues regarding the kitchen hearth:
first, to serve the *saṃgha* with all one's strength and with patience.
Second, one should regard those above and below with equal respect when practicing the Buddha-dharma.
Third, if someone comes seeking anything from you, you should give it all immediately; you must not refuse by saying that you have nothing.
Fourth, one should rise early and go out to inspect that everything is prepared.
Fifth, when sending others on errands or making purchases, one must not resort to begging for what is needed.
Sixth, when wishing to call someone, one must not call out loudly from a distance.
Seventh, in all activities, one must not allow objects or vessels to make a loud noise.
Eighth, one should act in a way that accords with the wishes of all people; one must not act according to one's own will, acting directly and forcefully.

Ninth, if someone brings food or any other items, whether in small or large quantities, one should immediately inform the assembly to offer a *dakṣiṇā* (blessing); one must not accept them alone and then dismiss the person.
Tenth: One should distribute [the food] so that it reaches everyone; even if the time for eating has passed, one should store it away rather than immediately inspecting it.
Eleventh: If a donor comes and says they wish to prepare a meal, but you have not yet seen what they possess, you must not speak of it immediately to others.

If the host brings money to provide a meal for the community of bhikṣus, you should give the bowl and the clay [for the water filter] to the host, or inform the virtuous ones to consult together on what should be done for both parties; you must not decide this alone.
Twelfth, when drawing water, one must not throw the jar into the well with great force, causing the water to become turbid.
Thirteenth, one must not personally select the rice grains.
Fourteenth, one must wash the cauldron three times, changing the water each time, until it is clean.
Fifteenth: Do not pour hot water from a cauldron onto the ground.
Sixteenth: One must not light a fire in the kitchen oneself.
Seventeenth: One must not personally sweep living grass or cut its roots.
Eighteenth: One must not place raw vegetable roots or leaves into the fire.
Nineteenth: One must not pour leftover rice into a ditch or stream.
Twentieth: All utensils for food should be covered so that they do not become covered in dust.
Twenty-first: One must not instruct others to prepare surplus portions; if the Sangha does not eat them, one should set them aside and discard them oneself.
Twenty-second: One must not take communal property for one's own personal use as a favor.
Twenty-third: One should personally inspect the storage containers and ensure they are securely fastened.
Twenty-fourth: One must not set aside food for today to be eaten on the following morning. Twenty-fifth:
One must not carry food intended for the following morning to be eaten on that same day.
There are seven matters for attending to newly arrived bhikṣus: first, upon their arrival, one should inquire after their well-being;

second, one should assign them a seat according to seniority; third, one should provide them with a dwelling; fourth, one should provide them with bedding, covers, and pillows; fifth, one should provide them with lamps and fire; sixth, one should inform them of the instructions and regulations of the bhikṣu-saṃgha; and seventh, one should inform them of the local customs of the country.
There are five matters for instructing others on how to engage in buying and selling:

first, one should instruct them not to quarrel with others; second, one should instruct them to buy what is pure; third, one must not allow them to encroach upon others; fourth, they must not run after or urge people in haste; fifth, they should protect the feelings of others.
There are five matters regarding the purchase of meat:
first, if one sees that the meat is whole and has not yet been cut, one should not purchase it;
second, only when another person has already cut it may one then purchase the remainder.
Third, even if one sees that there is little meat, one must not buy it all;
fourth, if the meat is scarce, one must not falsely increase the price to take it;
fifth, even if the meat has already been sold out, one must not say that one will purchase more later.
There are five matters regarding instructing others to draw water:

first, one must have them first clean the water vessel; second, one must have them place it in a secluded spot; third, one must cover it to keep it clean; fourth, one must not allow it to be defiled by oily liquids; fifth, if it has been defiled by anyone, it may not be used again.
There are five matters regarding the instruction of others in splitting firewood:

first, do not split it in the middle of a path; second, first examine the handle of the axe to ensure it is sturdy; third, do not allow green wood to be split; fourth, do not recklessly split materials intended for stupas; fifth, stack it in a dry location.
There are five matters for instructing others in the selection of rice:

first, one should personally measure and observe the quantity; second, there must be no weeds; third, one must pick out mouse droppings; fourth, one must not allow any unhusked grain to remain; fifth, one must face a clean area.
There are five matters for instructing others on how to rinse rice:
first, one should use a sturdy vessel; second, use pure water; third, change the water five times to ensure it is clean; fourth, place it in a secluded location; and fifth, cover it securely.
There are five matters regarding the washing of the cauldron:

first, one must not strike the bottom of the cauldron forcefully with the liquid; second, one should use a vessel with a lid to receive the wastewater and discard it; third, one should refill it with water until it is full; fourth, one should clean the wooden lid and cover it over the top; fifth, at dusk, one should cover it and inspect it to ensure it is secure.
There are five matters regarding the lighting of a hearth:

first, one must not place firewood crosswise; second, one must not light raw wood; third, one must not light a cauldron by placing wood upside down; fourth, one must not blow on the fire with one's mouth to make it burn; fifth, one must not extinguish the fire by pouring hot water over it.
There are five matters for instructing others on how to cook rice:
first, one should instruct them to wait until the steam emerges before arranging the grains;
second, as the steam rises, one should gradually stir the rice while it cooks.
Third, place the steamer upright so that steam cannot escape;
fourth, place the rice inside the steamer and immediately cover it;
fifth, once it is cooked, remove it and likewise keep it covered so that it is not exposed.
There are five matters regarding the selection of vegetables:

first, one must remove the roots; second, one must make them equal in size; third, one must not allow green and yellow parts to be mixed together; fourth, one must wash them clean; fifth, one must ensure they are all turned toward the fire so that they may be known [to be cooked], and only then may they be spread out for use.
There are five matters regarding the preparation of soup:

first, one should instruct [the cook] to add ingredients in the proper sequence; second, one should ensure it is cooked thoroughly; third, one should ensure the flavor is well-balanced; fourth, one should personally inspect it to ensure it is clean and pure; fifth, once it is cooked, one should remove it from the fire and cover it.
There are five matters for instructing others on washing the table and all utensils for food:

first, one must change the water three times to ensure it is clean; second, one must wipe them until they are clean; third, one must arrange the items on the table so that they are two feet apart from one another; fourth, one must place the table directly upon a sturdy stand to ensure it is stable; fifth, one must not allow the food to soil the robes of the bhikṣu-saṃgha.
There are five occasions for striking the *gandi*:

first, at the time of the regular assembly; second, at the time of the morning meal; third, at the time of the midday meal; fourth, at the time of evening recitation; and fifth, at the time of all impermanence.
Furthermore, there are seven matters:
first, government officials; second, great fires; third, great floods; fourth, bandits; fifth, assemblies of śrāmaṇeras; sixth, assemblies of upāsakas; and seventh, summoning one's own children.
Furthermore, one should know the procedure for the *gandī* at the twelve periods of the day:

at the regular assembly, it first begins with small strikes and gradually increases to large ones; when the large strikes are twenty, they gradually decrease to twenty-one small strikes, then ten very small strikes, and finally three large strikes again.
At dawn, there are eight strokes; during the day, one stroke for the meal, and one stroke when the bowl is set down.
For the assembly of śrāmaṇeras, there are three strokes; for upāsakas, three strokes; and for those who have passed away, it is according to the time observed.
The local officials, water, fire, and bandits also appear at their appointed times.
Summon a private servant once; he shall carry one strike of the *kaiṭi* (wooden gong) for the bhikṣus, with no further sound thereafter.
There are one hundred and sixty matters concerning the *pāṭimokkha* assembly, which Mopoli (Upāli) must practice.
When the *pāṭimokkha* assembly is held, there are five matters:

first, one must pay homage to the Buddha; second, one must pay homage to the Saṃgha; third, one must sit according to seniority; fourth, one must not sit heavily upon the seat making noise; fifth, one must leave space for the elders.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, one must not dispute over seating order;
second, one should show reverence toward the senior monks.
Third, one must comply with the regulations of the community;
fourth, if Mopoli is on duty that day, when he is assigned a task, one must accept it according to the Dharma;
fifth, once the work is finished, upon rising from one's seat, one must go and inform the Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
There are five matters for one who has already received the duty of the day:

first, one must first receive the keys to the doors; second, one must count the bronze Buddha images; third, one must count the bronze incense burners; fourth, one must count the bronze lamps; and fifth, one must properly arrange the seating mats and personally verify the records.
There are five matters regarding the sweeping of the stupa: first, one must not wear shoes upon it;

second, one must not sweep the stupa with one’s back turned toward the Buddha; third, one must not take soil from the upper part and discard it below; fourth, one should remove the withered flowers from atop the Buddha image; fifth, one should pass by to wash one's hands, take a clean cloth, and return.
There are five matters regarding the wiping of a Buddha image:

first, one should hold it firmly; second, one should constantly wipe it until it is clean; third, one must not use the hand to rub near the face or eyes, nor touch the fingers; fourth, one should personally provide money to purchase flowers; and fifth, one should distribute them to others so that they may scatter them over the Buddha.
There are five matters regarding the sweeping of beneath a stupa:

first, one should first sprinkle the ground; second, one should make it even; third, one should wait for it to dry; fourth, one must not sweep against the grain; fifth, one must not sweep against the wind.
There are five matters regarding sweeping: first, one must not remove the fine dust;

second, one should pick up the grass with one's own hands; third, one should take the soil from the center and move it toward the lower area; fourth, one must not leave visible tracks in the four corners of the swept area; fifth, one should sweep the six steps in front of the stupa until they are clean.
When convening an assembly of the great bhikṣu-saṃgha, there are seven matters for cleaning the lecture hall:
first, one should rise early and go to inspect whether the doors are open;
second, one should check the empty lamps and remove them.
Third, one should sweep and wipe the Buddha images and remove the flowers from the previous night;
fourth, one should burn incense before the Buddha;
fifth, one should light a great lamp in the center of the hall and arrange the seating mats for the assembly of bhikṣus.
Sixth, when the monks have finished their business and departed, one should slowly sprinkle water on the ground;
seventh, one should sweep the ground clean once more.
There are five matters regarding the sprinkling of water on the ground:

First, one should walk backward; second, one should move one's hands lightly; third, one should ensure it reaches everywhere; fourth, one should wait for it to dry; fifth, one must not splash anyone’s clothes.
There are five matters regarding the sweeping of the stupa grounds:
first, one must not sweep with one's back turned toward the Buddha;
second, if the area is large, one must not swing the broom about and soil others' feet.
Third, one must not sweep away the topsoil;
fourth, one should remove it with one's own hands and discard it;
fifth, one must not place it where people walk, nor discard it in water or in the latrine.

There are five matters regarding the inspection of lamps: first, one must not extinguish the central wick; second, one should pour out the remaining oil from within and use it to make a large lamp to burn before the Buddha; third, one should take the empty lamp and place it back in its usual location; fourth, one must not recklessly break or shatter it; fifth, if any items are lost, one must purchase replacements and restore them to their usual locations.
There are three matters regarding the burning of incense before the Buddha:
first, one should replace the old embers; second, one should personally take out the incense; third, one should distribute it to others.
There are three matters for arranging the bedding and seats of the bhikṣu-saṃgha:
first, one should inspect the legs of the beds to ensure they are secure;
second, one should sweep and wipe them down with a sincere mind to make them clean.
Third, when wiping the mat, one should do so thoroughly so as not to soil the robes of the bhikṣu-saṃgha.
There are three matters regarding the preparation of the incense burner:
first, one must first remove the old embers and gather the remaining incense to one side.
Second, one should wipe it clean before placing it over the fire, then take the old incense and place it back inside;
third, when placing it over the fire, the flame must not be too intense nor too weak, lest the embers quickly die out and become dark.
There are five matters regarding the lighting of a lamp:
first, one should use a clean cloth to wipe both the interior and exterior to make them pure;
second, one should prepare a pure wick.
Third, one should prepare the sesame oil oneself;
fourth, when applying the ointment, it must neither be applied too full nor too thin;
fifth, one should protect it so that it remains firm, ensuring it does not hang down, obstruct people's paths, or defile others.
This is the method for the day-duty officer; by practicing as described above, one shall obtain merit.
The foregoing are the sixty matters to be performed by the day-duty officer.
The *māmaka* possesses fifteen virtues:
First, because of the Buddha;
second, because of the Dharma;
third, because of the community of bhikṣus.
Fourth, because of the Upādhyāya and Ācārya;
fifth, because of me having left the household life to become a śramaṇa;
sixth, because of acting as a host and enduring those from the four distant quarters.
Seventh, one must wait for those from the four distant regions;
eighth, if someone among the assembly commits an offense, one must not privately punish them before others;
ninth, if one person among the assembly commits an offense and the multitude wishes to punish him, one should descend from one's seat to request it on his behalf and must not conceal it alone.
Tenth, one should possess virtue;
eleventh, one should be able to attract donors;
twelfth, when bhikṣus from the four distant regions arrive with tattered robes and coverlets, one should beg for and provide them with patches and mends.
Thirteenth, all food and drink should be shared in common;
fourteenth, one should attend equally to those who are ill or emaciated;
fifteenth, upon hearing that there is a sick bhikṣu outside, one should go to visit and care for him.

Furthermore, there are six matters: first, one must not take property belonging to the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* (the universal community of monks) and place it with property belonging to a stūpa; second, one must not take property belonging to the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* and place it with property belonging to the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*; third, one must not take property belonging to a stūpa and place it with property belonging to the *cātuddisa-saṃgha*; fourth, one must not take property belonging to a stūpa and place it with property belonging to the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*; fifth, one must not take property belonging to the *bhikṣu-saṃgha* and place it with property belonging to a stūpa; sixth, one must not take property belonging to the *bhikṣu-saṃgha* and place it with property belonging to the *cātuddisa-saṃgha*.
Furthermore, there are three matters:
first, regarding everything from a single hair to countless things, one must not conceal anything.

Second, from the novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) up to the *āyuṣmat*, if anyone suffers from illness or their robes and bedding are damaged, one should purchase replacements for them; one must not provide these as a favor to seek fame or reputation, but should ensure that all such actions are performed with equanimity.

Third, regarding all items belonging to a stūpa or property belonging to the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters (cāturdisa-saṃgha), one must not enter or exit [the monastery] while handling them; such persons as these shall not first receive the merit from those offerings.
One who is able to protect these matters may serve as the *karmadāna*.
Furthermore, there are four matters:

first, from the fifteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the seventh month, one should calculate together with the community of bhikṣus and prepare a detailed register of all items to be reported.
Having thus calculated [the time], everyone knows the essential point: all that remains must be viewed as clearly manifest in the present.

Second, from the fifteenth day until the next fifteenth day, whether it be Māpali or the Saṃgha together, they calculate and examine the register while contemplating impermanence; these constitute the four practices.

Third, if a bhikṣu wishes to arrive at that place and stay overnight, he should inquire about three matters: the stūpa, the Buddha image, or the various items belonging to the Saṅgha; whether it is the Bhikṣu-saṅgha; or the name of the day, the patron’s surname and given name—all such inquiries must be answered so that they may be fully informed.
Fourth, if a national dignitary, an elder, the head of a monastery, or a donor brings offerings, whether large or small, one must immediately inform the Sangha so that all may hear of them.
These four matters, which the worthy one encounters without begrudging, constitute the merit and efficacy of a *karmadāna*; through self-purification, one attains the path to transcendence.
The steward possesses ten virtues:
first, he exerts his full effort for the sake of the three dharmas;
second, if there are bhikṣus coming from afar, he should go out to meet them and ensure their well-being.
Third, one should provide bedding and seats, as well as lamps and fire, for three days up to seven days.
Fourth, if the rooms are all full, one should vacate them oneself and give one's own quarters to others.
Fifth, one should frequently go to inquire after his health and observe him.
Sixth, one should explain for him the customs and traditions of the country.
Seventh, one should take concern for whatever he lacks.
Eighth, if there are disputes among those in the midst of the community, one must not take sides; one should always strive for reconciliation so that all may be at peace and secure.

Ninth, if someone has been unfriendly toward you in the past, you must not revile or scold them in the midst of the assembly, nor should you summon others to join you in doing something that would cause the leader displeasure.

Tenth, one must not engage in disputes with Māpali to seek out his faults, nor should one repeatedly speak of such matters within the assembly; furthermore, one must not take any of the items belonging to the Three Dharma [Treasures] and carry them away as a personal favor.
One who practices according to the Dharma may serve as the steward (*śayanāsana-grāhaka*).
By what causes and conditions do all things arise?
There are five factors:
First, the four seasons and five elements; second, the spiritual lineage; third, spontaneity; fourth, giving; and fifth, merit.
By means of these five matters, the Director of the Year shall inevitably attain Buddhahood.
There are five matters for which the *duṇḍubhi* (wooden gong) is struck:

first, for a formal assembly; second, for the regular assembly to recite the scriptures; third, for the *poṣadha*; fourth, for the assembly of monks to take a meal; and fifth, for all matters concerning impermanence.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, when striking the *gandi*, one should first observe whether it is early or late;
second, one should always inform the *upādhyāya* (preceptor).
Third, one must wait for the donor to see whether the requisites for the *parinirvāṇa* have been prepared;
fourth, one must act in accordance with the wishes of the assembly;
fifth, one must occupy a seat according to seniority in the monastic order and must not rise from one's seat repeatedly.

Furthermore, there are five matters: first, one must not sit directly facing the Sangha; second, one must not personally impose fines upon others; third, one’s speech should always accord with the wishes of others; fourth, when reporting matters, one must not increase or decrease the words of others; fifth, if there is anything to be distributed, it must all be apportioned equitably.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, if there is one who acts contrary to the Dharma within the Sangha, one should not immediately revile or scold them in the midst of the assembly;
second, one must not disobey the legitimate commands of the Sangha.
Third, one must not repeatedly leave the Sangha to act recklessly;

fourth, when the task is completed, one should confess before the Sangha, and if there are objections regarding the speech or the distribution was unequal, one should request absolution for the offense;
fifth, after having made the formal announcement (*jñapti*) to them, one must not depart first.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, one should visit and attend to those who are ill or emaciated every morning and evening;
second, one should go daily to inquire after the health of the elders and other dignitaries.
Third, one should go at the appropriate time to the house of a donor to inquire after their welfare;
fourth, if a bhikṣu arrives from afar, one should provide him with comfort and security;
fifth, if a fellow student passes away, one should oversee the funeral arrangements and escort the remains to a distant place for interment.
These are the twenty-five virtues of Dhumāpāli.
From these five virtues:
first, in whatever place you are born in future lives, if you should fall ill and be confined to bed, there shall naturally be one who carries divine medicine to attend to and protect you.
Second, if in a future life one should find oneself in a place of hardship and distress where nothing can be heard or known, there shall naturally be someone who calls out to them.
Third, if in a future life one should find oneself in a place devoid of grain, water, or drink, there shall naturally be someone who brings fragrant, sweet, and delicious food to give to them.
Fourth, if in a future life they should find themselves in an unstable place, suffering from hunger and thirst, there shall spontaneously appear one who brings them ambrosia (*amṛta*).
Fifth, having already received this merit, they shall in a future life surely attain the path and the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*).
When striking the *gandī* for an assembly, one should first begin with the small strikes: thirty large strikes, followed by twenty, then ten, and finally five small strikes.
This was repeated three times; thereafter, he had three major purgings.
When he met with the śramaṇas, he had forty major purgings, followed by thirty, then twenty, then ten, and finally five minor purgings.
For the three upper [vows], one descends by three great units;

for the latter three, one descends by seven small units, then fifty great units, then forty, then thirty, then twenty, and finally ten small units. At the time of the *poṣadha*, one first performs these small and great descents.
There are also three "passings through" (tōng), with four "large descents" (dà xià) at the beginning.

When the Sangha eats, first there are four large descents; then twenty direct descents (shū zhí xià); next ten small descents; then another ten very small descents; next five descents; and finally, two more passings through.
First, regarding the counting according to the occasion, one should observe the causes and conditions for the three types of intervals.
When it is not a fixed time, there is no counting; sometimes one is urgent at first and relaxed later, or sometimes relaxed at first and urgent later. This is the *dharmaghaṇṭā* method of Duḥmāpāli.
There shall be five matters:
first, upon hearing the sound of the *gandi*, one should immediately don the *kāṣāya*, exit the room according to the Dharma;
second, one should stand outside the lecture hall, straighten the *kāṣāya*, remove the cap, and then enter.
Third, where there is an image of the Buddha, one should prostrate with the head touching the ground, and having performed that salutation, proceed to pay respects to the Sangha;
fourth, one should follow the proper order toward the senior monk (upādhyāya);
fifth, one should leave space for the senior monk, and as the senior monk sits down, one should squat accordingly.
There are five matters regarding sitting in a squatting posture (*utkuṭukāsana*):

first, one must not cross the feet; second, one must not place both feet forward together; third, one must not squat with both hands behind and swing the two feet about; fourth, one must not prop up one foot while extending the other; fifth, one must not place one foot above the other.

There are five matters regarding sitting upright: first, one must not lean against a wall; second, one must not rest both hands on the knees in front; third, one must not rest the elbows on the seat; fourth, one must not lie prostrate with both hands cupping the head; fifth, one must not prop the cheek with the fingers.

Furthermore, there are five matters: first, one must not lean against the shoulders of those to one's left or right; second, one must not rise recklessly to sit at the edge of the seat before the *upādhyāya* or *sthavira*; third, one must not recklessly scold or reprimand the *mānavaka* or those of lower rank; fourth, one must not remove one’s *kāṣāya* and leave the *sthavira’s* quarters wearing it; fifth, one must not sit shaking oneself so that the bed makes a sound.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, when about to go out, one should first straighten the *kāṣāya* so that it is not uneven;
second, when straightening the *kāṣāya*, one should look to the left and right to ensure it does not brush against another's face.
Third, when rising, one must look at the ground, not more than six feet ahead;
fourth, when rising and stepping out, one must not allow the *kāṣāya* to touch the ground;
fifth, when walking, one must gaze straight ahead and must not look left or right.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, when a senior elder (*sthavira*) preaches the sutras, one must not correct him from below.
Second, even if the senior elder should engage in a dispute with another, one must not assist him from below.
Third, when a junior monk engages in a dispute or has something to report, one must not forcefully rebuke or stop him.
Fourth, when Mopali comes forward with something to report, the senior monk should immediately rise from his seat, move to a lower seat, and say "Yes."

Fifth, one must not say, "The elder so-and-so was next in line to perform [a duty], but the junior monk so-and-so constantly pointed it out and acted for me," nor should one say, "I myself previously performed such-and-such.
Furthermore, there are five other matters:
first, once one has informed another that they have departed, one must not later say, "What so-and-so did today was merely acting willfully and arbitrarily."
Second, one must not say, "I wish to challenge such-and-such person today," or "I merely wish to employ such-and-such person, so I am leaving him aside.
Third, when the *upādhyāya* or *ācārya* has something to pass on, one should follow it; if they instruct you to go first to fetch something, you should receive their instructions exactly as spoken.

Fourth, if returning together with [the teacher], one must not enter the gate before him; one should follow behind, keeping to the right side. If traveling during the day, one must not step upon the teacher’s shadow.
Fifth, if someone wishes to detain one for a meal, one should inform the teacher before departing; one must not allow oneself to be detained for a meal.
Furthermore, there are five matters:

first, if someone insists on sitting with one to provide a meal and it is impossible to inform the teacher, one should seek to leave immediately after the meal is finished; one must not remain seated until dusk.
Second, if you return at dusk, you must recount the events as they occurred and confess your transgressions.
Third, you must not praise yourself in private, saying:
"Today a certain person invited me alone to stay for a meal; there was nothing they did not provide."
Fourth, one must not say in front of others:
"I intended to return home for a meal today, but so-and-so forcibly detained me for a meal, causing discomfort within my stomach."

"Fifth, one should instead practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) and enter the room to contemplate and reflect upon the Path; one must not arbitrarily enter the rooms of others to discuss worldly matters.
When entering the assembly during the *poṣadha* ceremony, there are five things that must not be done:

first, one must not wear leather sandals when entering the assembly; second, one must not lean on a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*) when entering the assembly; third, one must not carry a bamboo fan or a white hand-towel when entering the assembly; fourth, one must not wear white shoes when entering the assembly; and fifth, one must not wear wooden clogs when entering the assembly."
Furthermore, there are five matters:
First, when the community of bhikṣus assembles, one must not enter among the ranks wearing only a tied-up *kāṣāya*.
Second, one must not stand before the door of the lecture hall to observe the monks.
Third, one must not squat outside the door and listen to the monks' conversation.
Fourth, one must not stand in the doorway and shout loudly to detain the venerable ones.
Fifth, even if the doors of the lecture hall are closed, one must not push them open; if one wishes to enter urgently, one should snap the fingers three times.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, once one has already recited the sutras and precepts, one should not perform prostrations again.
Second, one should keep the head lowered, proceeding from top to bottom until reaching the seat.
Third, one must not displace or seize another's seat.
Fourth, one must not speak of external worldly matters.
Fifth, once seated, one must not say to the bhikṣu-saṃgha, "Why has today’s assembly gathered so early?"

Furthermore, there are five matters: first, when deliberating on affairs with others, one must not speak frivolously; second, one must not spit recklessly upon the ground before one; third, one must not rest one's hands upon one's knees; fourth, one must not sleep with one's hands supporting one's head; fifth, one must not yawn with the mouth wide open.
Upon arriving behind the dwelling, there are twenty-five matters:
first, when one wishes to relieve oneself and is about to depart, one must not perform prostrations to the senior monks (*upādhyāya*) on the path.
Second, one must likewise not receive prostrations from others.
Third, when approaching, one should always keep the head slightly bowed and gaze at the ground.
Fourth, upon approaching, one should snap the fingers three times.
Fifth, if others have already snapped their fingers, one must not press forward.
Sixth, having already settled into one's place, one should squat only after snapping the fingers three times.
Seventh, one must squat in the center.
Eighth, one must not have one foot forward and the other foot drawn back.
Ninth, one must not lean the body against anything.
Tenth, one must gather up one's robes so that they do not hang down into the toilet.
Eleventh, one must not swallow loudly or cause the face to turn red.
12. One should gaze straight ahead and must not look back or listen.
13. One must not spit and defile the four walls.
14. One must not lower one's head to look into the latrine.
Fifteenth, one must not gaze at the private parts.
Sixteenth, one must not hold the private parts with the hand.
Seventeenth, one must not hold grass and draw characters on the ground.
Eighteenth: One must not take grass and draw characters upon a wall.
Nineteenth: When using water, one must not waste it excessively.
Twentieth: One must not splash or soil [the surroundings].
Twenty-first: when using water, one must not allow the front hand to touch the back hand.
Twenty-second: when using earth, one should apply it three times.
Twenty-third: one should use cleansing powder (*śāṭī*).
Twenty-fourth: [the water] must be strained three times. Twenty-fifth:
if one sees that the water, plants, or soil are all exhausted, one should inform the person in charge of the day’s duties; it is virtuous if one takes [the remaining materials] with one's own hand.
There are ten circumstances in which one should not use water:

first, when performing work for a stūpa; second, when performing work for the community of bhikṣus; third, during extreme cold; fourth, while walking on the path; fifth, when not using the latrine together with a woman; sixth, when intending to rise from one's seat to recite a sūtra; seventh, when copying a sūtra; eighth, when making a dharma robe; ninth, when dyeing a robe; tenth, when about to travel far and has been invited [to a meal]. In these cases, one must not use water;
however, if there is fragrant grass available, one may use water.
There are ten matters concerning the arousal of the *kāmacchanda* (sensual desire), five of which are culpable and five of which are non-culpable:

first, arousal upon seeing a form; second, arousal due to hearing about causes and conditions; third, arousal from contemplating the physical beauty of a woman; fourth, arousal from recollecting past causes and conditions; fifth, arousal when holding something in one's hand—these are culpable.

There is no offense in the following cases: first, when one is lying down and stretching; second, when it is habitual; third, when one is lying down and yawning; fourth, when there is a sore on the body and one holds [the organ] close with the hand; fifth, when one wishes to urinate but is unable to grasp it due to being pressed, and the organ becomes erect—there is no offense.
From the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month constitutes one period; these one hundred and twenty days belong to winter.
From the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month constitutes one period; these one hundred and twenty days belong to spring.
From the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month constitutes one period; these one hundred and twenty days belong to summer and mark the end of the long year.
From the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month belongs to winter.
Having become a śramaṇa, if one does not undergo the summer retreat, although one may obtain the *pārvana*, one does not obtain the *varṣā* (the year-end reckoning).
There are some śramaṇas who obtain the *varṣā* on the fifteenth day, and others who obtain it on the sixteenth day.
The Sarvāstivādins are broadly learned and possess quick intelligence; they guide and benefit others through the transformation of the Dharma and should wear saffron-colored *kāṣāyas*.
The Dharmaguptakas uphold the weighty precepts and sever worldly laws; they should wear black *kāṣāyas*.
The Kāśyapīya school, being diligent, courageous, and decisive in rescuing and protecting sentient beings, should wear saffron-colored (*mūlana*) kashāyas.
The Mahīśāsaka school, which contemplates in meditation to penetrate the subtle and fully elucidate the profound mysteries, should wear blue kashāyas.
The Mahāsaṃghikas are those who diligently study the various sūtras and expound their meanings and principles; they should wear yellow *kāṣāyas*.
In the past, when the Buddha was present, the members of the assembly wore robes that were purely and simply colored, not mixed with white.

After this, there was a bhikṣu named Rāhula who always returned empty-handed from his almsrounds. The Buddha, knowing of his past offenses and wishing to demonstrate the consequences of misfortune and fortune as a clear warning for future generations, divided the community of monks into five divisions, each wearing robes of one of the five colors; thus, the established regulations were subsequently inherited.
Until after the Buddha has passed into Nirvāṇa, let us establish a title and adopt this long-standing name for our community.
All you who have gathered here, please listen with patience!

Now, as the Bhikṣus plan for the four directions, regarding all auspicious responses and remaining karmic duties, may the assembly of monks together harmoniously accept and endure them. Thus, with one voice, we shall be single-mindedly diligent in the prohibitions and precepts, practicing equanimity and purely guarding all the trainings.

Now, regarding this boundary-establishment, you should all listen with patience to these instructions and together plan the measurements for the four directions, so that the prohibitions may be proclaimed and the boundary of the vihāra established.
If you are able to do so, remain entirely silent;
if you cannot accept it, then speak out.
At the assembly of the Saṃgha, having together with focused diligence established the boundary of equality, the prohibitions and precepts were proclaimed.
The Saṃgha approved them and maintained them in silence.
